questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the term 'State' in Article 12:
1. It includes local authorities such as municipalities and panchayats.
2. In Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mubarak (1981), the Supreme Court laid down tests to decide whether a body is an instrumentality or agency of the State.
3. In Zee Telefilms (2005), the Supreme Court held that the BCCI is 'State' under Article 12.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 12 covers Government and Parliament, State governments and legislatures, local authorities and 'other authorities', and Ajay Hasia supplied the tests for the last group (funding, deep and pervasive control, functional character). In Zee Telefilms the Court held that the BCCI is not 'State', although it can face a writ under Article 226 for public functions.

questions.q:
Match the cases with their holdings on 'other authorities' in Article 12.
A. Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagat Ram (1975)  B. Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mubarak (1981)  C. Zee Telefilms v. Union of India (2005)
1. Statutory corporations such as LIC, ONGC and IFC are 'State'
2. A society can be 'State' if it is an instrumentality of the Government
3. The BCCI is not 'State'
questions.e: Sukhdev Singh brought statutory corporations within Article 12; Ajay Hasia extended this to a registered society that satisfies the instrumentality tests; Zee Telefilms refused to treat the BCCI as State.
questions.h: Sukhdev = Statutory; Ajay = Agency tests; Zee = BCCI Zero.

questions.q: Which one of the following sets of Articles can be enforced even against private individuals, and not only against the State?
questions.e: Fundamental Rights are generally claimed against the State. The exceptions are the bar on discrimination in access to shops, wells and public places (Art 15(2)), abolition of untouchability (Art 17), and the prohibition of forced labour and child labour (Arts 23 and 24).

questions.q: For the purposes of Article 13, 'law' includes all of the following EXCEPT
o: a constitutional amendment made under Article 368
a custom or usage having the force of law
questions.e: Article 13(3) includes ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications and customs having the force of law. Clause (4), added by the 24th Amendment, excludes Article 368 amendments, though Kesavananda Bharati makes them subject to the basic structure.

questions.q:
Statement-I: A pre-Constitution law that is inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is not dead but remains dormant, and revives if the inconsistency is removed.
Statement-II: A law made after the commencement of the Constitution that violates a Fundamental Right is void from its inception.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Statement-I is the doctrine of eclipse (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras, 1955): the old law is only overshadowed. Statement-II follows Deep Chand (1959), under which post-Constitution laws are still-born. They are independent propositions; the second does not explain the first.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. If one provision of a law violates a Fundamental Right, the whole law is void even if that provision can be separated from the rest.
2. Under the doctrine of severability, only the part of a law that violates a Fundamental Right is void, if it can be separated from the rest.
3. Under the doctrine of waiver, a person can voluntarily waive a Fundamental Right.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Article 13 makes a law void 'to the extent' of the inconsistency, which is the basis of severability. In Basheshar Nath (1959), the Court held that Fundamental Rights cannot be waived, since they are also a matter of public policy.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. In Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights because an amendment is 'law' under Article 13.
2. The 24th Amendment Act, 1971 inserted clause (4) in Article 13.
3. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Court overruled Golaknath and held that amendments under Article 368 are not 'law' under Article 13, but cannot alter the basic structure.
4. Golaknath was decided by a bench of thirteen judges.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: Parliament responded to Golaknath with the 24th Amendment, and Kesavananda settled the issue with the basic structure limit. Golaknath was decided by an eleven-judge bench; the thirteen-judge bench was in Kesavananda.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 14:
1. The concept of 'equality before law' is borrowed from the American Constitution.
2. 'Equal protection of the laws' means that like persons must be treated alike in like circumstances.
3. A classification is valid only if it rests on an intelligible differentia and has a rational nexus with the object of the law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: 'Equality before law' is British in origin and negative (no special privileges); 'equal protection of the laws' is American and positive. Reasonable classification, tested through the two-part test, is permitted.

questions.q: Which one of the following does NOT enjoy any special immunity from ordinary legal proceedings, as an exception to the rule of equality before law?
o: A Member of Parliament, for anything said in the House
questions.e: Under Article 361 the President and Governors are not answerable to any court for the exercise of their powers, and Article 105 protects speech in Parliament. The Chief Minister has no such immunity.

questions.q: Which one of the following cases first stated that arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality under Article 14?
o: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952)
E. P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974)
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
questions.e: Royappa gave the 'new concept' of equality: an arbitrary State action offends Article 14. Anwar Ali Sarkar dealt with the reasonable classification test, and Maneka Gandhi (1978) developed Royappa further.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 14 is available to citizens as well as non-citizens.
2. Article 14 prohibits every classification of persons by law.
3. Equality before law means that no one is above the ordinary law of the land, subject to constitutional exceptions.
4. Article 14 restrains only legislative action and not executive action.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Only statements 1 and 3 are correct, because Article 14 uses the word 'person' and reflects the rule of law. It forbids class legislation but allows reasonable classification, and it binds executive action as well.

questions.q:
Statement-I: A foreign national residing in India can invoke Article 14 of the Constitution.
Statement-II: Article 14 uses the word 'person' and not 'citizen'.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Because the Article protects every 'person' within India's territory, it is not limited to citizens, which explains why a foreigner can claim equality before law.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 15:
1. Article 15(1) prohibits the State from discriminating against citizens on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
2. Article 15(2) applies only to the State and not to private individuals.
3. Article 15(3) permits the State to make special provisions for women and children.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 15(2) bars any disability in access to shops, restaurants, wells, roads and similar places, and operates against private persons too. The word 'only' in Article 15(1) matters: discrimination on these grounds combined with other reasons is not barred by it.

questions.q:
Match the Amendments with the clauses of Article 15 they inserted.
A. First Amendment, 1951  B. 93rd Amendment, 2005  C. 103rd Amendment, 2019
1. Special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs
2. Reservation in admission to educational institutions, including private unaided ones other than minority institutions
3. Reservation for economically weaker sections, up to ten per cent
questions.e: The clauses were added in order: 15(4) by the First Amendment, 15(5) by the 93rd and 15(6) by the 103rd.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) reservation:
1. The Supreme Court in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022) unanimously upheld the 103rd Amendment.
2. The ten per cent EWS quota under Article 15(6) does not apply to minority educational institutions.
3. The EWS quota is meant for sections other than SCs, STs and the socially and educationally backward classes already covered by reservations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The 103rd Amendment was upheld in 2022 by a 3:2 majority, not unanimously. Article 15(6) excludes minority institutions and benefits those not covered by the existing reservations.
questions.s: Laxmikanth Ch 7; Janhit Abhiyan v. UoI (Nov 2022)

questions.q: The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 inserted clause (4) in Article 15 in response to which case?
o: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
M. R. Balaji v. State of Mysore
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
questions.e: The Supreme Court in Champakam Dorairajan struck down the communal allocation of seats in colleges as violating Articles 15(1) and 29(2). Parliament responded by inserting Article 15(4) so that the State could make special provisions for backward classes.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 102nd Amendment Act, 2018 gave constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes.
2. In Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister of Maharashtra (2021), the Supreme Court held that, after the 102nd Amendment, States could not identify socially and educationally backward classes for the Central list.
3. The 105th Amendment Act, 2021 restored the power of States and Union Territories to prepare their own lists of socially and educationally backward classes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The 102nd Amendment inserted Articles 338B and 342A. The 2021 ruling, which also set aside the Maratha quota, read Article 342A as giving the President the power to specify classes for the Central list, and the 105th Amendment then restored the States' power for their own lists.

questions.q: A State Government opens a polytechnic exclusively for girls and reserves a share of seats in other polytechnics for women. Which provision of the Constitution protects this from a challenge based on discrimination on grounds of sex?
questions.e: Article 15(1) bars discrimination on grounds of sex, but Article 15(3) is an exception that permits special provisions for women and children. Clause (4) is for backward classes and Article 16(4) concerns public employment.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 16:
1. The grounds on which discrimination is prohibited in Article 16(2) are identical to those in Article 15(1).
2. 'Descent' and 'residence' are grounds in Article 16(2) but not in Article 15(1).
3. Parliament, and not a State Legislature, can by law prescribe a residence requirement for appointment to a State public office.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 16(2) adds 'descent' and 'residence' to the Article 15 grounds, so the lists are not identical. Under Article 16(3), only Parliament can make a residence-based requirement, as it did in the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992):
1. The Court upheld the 27 per cent reservation for Other Backward Classes in Central Government jobs.
2. It held that the 50 per cent ceiling on reservation is absolute and admits of no exceptions.
3. It upheld reservation in promotions as permitted by Article 16(4).
4. It held that the creamy layer must be excluded among Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Only statement 1 is correct. The nine-judge bench allowed a 50 per cent ceiling subject to exceptions in extraordinary situations, did not allow reservation in promotions (with a five-year protection), and applied the creamy layer exclusion to OBCs.
questions.h: Indra: 27, 50, no promotion, creamy for OBC.

questions.q:
Match the Constitutional Amendments with their provisions on reservation in public employment.
A. 77th Amendment (1995)  B. 81st Amendment (2000)  C. 82nd Amendment (2000)  D. 85th Amendment (2001)
1. Carry forward of unfilled reserved vacancies as a separate class
2. Reservation in promotion for SCs and STs
3. Relaxation in qualifying marks and evaluation standards
4. Consequential seniority for reserved category promotees
questions.e: The 77th Amendment added Article 16(4A) after Indra Sawhney removed promotion quotas, the 81st added 16(4B), the 82nd amended Article 335 and the 85th gave consequential seniority.

questions.q: In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional amendments on reservation in promotion, but required that the State must first show
o: only that the class is socially backward, without data on representation
that the post is above Group C in the service
compelling reasons such as backwardness, inadequacy of representation and overall administrative efficiency
that the amendment has been ratified by half of the State Legislatures
questions.e: Nagaraj made the enabling provisions valid, but the exercise of the power needed quantifiable data on backwardness and inadequate representation and a check on administrative efficiency under Article 335. Ratification by States is not a requirement for these amendments.

questions.q:
Statement-I: The ten per cent reservation under Article 16(6) for economically weaker sections is in addition to the existing reservations for SCs, STs and OBCs.
Statement-II: Persons belonging to SCs, STs and OBCs are also eligible for the EWS reservation.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Article 16(6), inserted by the 103rd Amendment, creates a separate quota for economically weaker sections who are not covered by the existing reservation schemes. Those who already enjoy the SC, ST or OBC quotas are excluded from it.

questions.q:
Arrange the following in chronological order.
A. Indra Sawhney judgment  B. Appointment of the Mandal Commission  C. 77th Constitutional Amendment  D. Announcement of 27 per cent OBC reservation in Central jobs by the V. P. Singh Government
questions.e: The Mandal Commission was appointed in 1979, the V. P. Singh Government announced the OBC quota in 1990, the Supreme Court decided Indra Sawhney in 1992, and the 77th Amendment followed in 1995.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 17:
1. Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.
2. The Constitution defines 'untouchability' in Article 17.
3. Article 17 can be enforced only against the State and not against private individuals.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Article 17 does not define untouchability, and it operates against private individuals as well as the State. Parliament punishes its practice through a law made under Article 35.

questions.q: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 was originally enacted under which name?
o: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1955
questions.e: The Act, passed to give effect to Article 17, was originally the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955. It was renamed in 1976 and made stricter, while the 1989 Atrocities Act is a separate law.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 18:
1. Article 18 prohibits the State from conferring any title, including military or academic distinctions.
2. A citizen of India cannot accept any title from a foreign State.
3. A non-citizen holding an office of profit under the State needs the consent of the President to accept a title from a foreign State.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 18 forbids titles except military or academic distinctions, so statement 1 is wrong. The bar on foreign titles for citizens, and the need for presidential consent for non-citizen office holders, are correct.

questions.q: In Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996), the Supreme Court held that the national awards like Bharat Ratna and the Padma awards
o: may be used as a suffix to the awardee's name
are not 'titles' under Article 18(1), but should not be used as a prefix or suffix to the name
are valid only if awarded for military distinction
questions.e: The Court held these awards are 'decorations' and not titles that create a separate class. They cannot be used as prefix or suffix, and misuse can lead to forfeiture.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 19:
1. Article 19(1) currently guarantees seven freedoms.
2. The right to property was deleted from Article 19(1) by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.
3. The 97th Amendment Act, 2011 added 'co-operative societies' to the right to form associations or unions.
4. The freedoms in Article 19 are available to all persons, including foreigners.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Only statements 2 and 3 are correct. Six freedoms remain, since 19(1)(f) on property was deleted, and Article 19 is available only to citizens.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the grounds for restricting freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(2):
1. 'Sovereignty and integrity of India' was added as a ground by the 16th Amendment Act, 1963.
2. 'Public order' was an original ground in the Constitution.
3. 'Friendly relations with foreign States' and 'incitement to an offence' were added by the First Amendment Act, 1951.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The First Amendment, passed after Romesh Thappar and Brij Bhushan, added public order, friendly relations with foreign States and incitement to an offence. The 16th Amendment added sovereignty and integrity.
questions.h: 1st: P-F-I (Public order, Friendly relations, Incitement); 16th: Sovereignty.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a ground for imposing reasonable restrictions on freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(2)?
questions.e: Article 19(2) lists sovereignty and integrity, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence. Public health is not listed.

questions.q:
Match the cases with the principle laid down.
A. Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950)  B. Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)  C. Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020)  D. Naveen Jindal v. Union of India (2004)
1. Freedom of the press is part of freedom of speech and expression
2. Section 66A of the Information Technology Act was struck down as vague and overbroad
3. Freedom of speech through the internet and trade over the internet are protected, and indefinite shutdowns are impermissible
4. The right to fly the national flag is a form of expression
questions.e: Each case anchors a part of Article 19(1)(a): the press (Romesh Thappar), free speech online (Shreya Singhal, Anuradha Bhasin) and symbolic expression (Naveen Jindal).

questions.q:
Statement-I: The right to strike is a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(c).
Statement-II: The freedom to form associations or unions includes the right to form trade unions.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: The Supreme Court in T. K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu (2003) held that there is no fundamental right to strike. The right to form associations and unions is, however, protected by Article 19(1)(c).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Restrictions on the freedom to reside and settle in any part of India can be imposed for the protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe.
2. Article 19(6) permits the State to prescribe professional or technical qualifications for practising a profession.
3. A citizen has an absolute fundamental right to carry on a trade even if the State has created a monopoly in it by law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 19(5) allows restrictions in the interests of the general public or of a Scheduled Tribe, and Article 19(6) allows qualifications and a State monopoly. Hence the freedom to trade is subject to the State monopoly.

questions.q: An order suspends internet services in a district for an indefinite period on grounds of law and order. In the light of Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020), which one of the following is correct?
o: The State may suspend the internet indefinitely, since public order overrides Article 19
Internet suspension is a purely executive matter and cannot be reviewed by courts
Access to the internet is an absolute right and cannot be restricted at all
An indefinite suspension is impermissible; orders must be published, necessary, proportionate, limited in time and open to judicial review
questions.e: The Court held that freedom of speech through the internet and the freedom to trade online are protected by Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g), subject to reasonable restrictions. It required proportionality, publication of orders and judicial review.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Fundamental Rights during a National Emergency:
1. The freedoms under Article 19 are automatically suspended when an Emergency is declared on grounds of war or external aggression.
2. Article 19 is also automatically suspended when an Emergency is declared on the ground of armed rebellion.
3. The President cannot suspend the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 by an order under Article 359.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: After the 44th Amendment, Article 358 applies only to war or external aggression, not armed rebellion, and Articles 20 and 21 can no longer be suspended under Article 359.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 20:
1. Article 20(1) prohibits conviction for an act that was not an offence under the law in force when it was committed.
2. Article 20(1) prohibits the imposition of a penalty greater than that prescribed by the law at the time of the offence.
3. Article 20(1) prohibits retrospective tax and civil liability.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: The protection against ex post facto laws in Article 20(1) applies only to criminal laws. Retrospective civil and tax laws are not barred by it.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the protection against double jeopardy under Article 20(2):
1. It applies only where the person was prosecuted and punished earlier before a court or judicial tribunal.
2. A departmental inquiry followed by a criminal prosecution for the same act violates Article 20(2).
3. It bars a second civil suit on the same cause of action.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Article 20(2) requires both prosecution and punishment in a judicial proceeding, so departmental action does not bar a later prosecution. It does not apply to civil proceedings.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the protection against self-incrimination under Article 20(3):
1. In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court held that the involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests violates Article 20(3).
2. Compelling an accused to give fingerprints or handwriting samples violates Article 20(3).
3. Article 20(3) protects a person accused of an offence from being compelled to be a witness against himself.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Selvi treated these tests as testimonial compulsion, as they reveal personal knowledge. In Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961), however, giving specimen handwriting or fingerprints was held not to be testimony, since it is physical evidence.

questions.q:
Statement-I: The protection under Article 20 remains available even during a National Emergency.
Statement-II: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 provided that the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended by a Presidential order under Article 359.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: The 44th Amendment limited the Emergency powers, which ensures that Articles 20 and 21 stay enforceable throughout, so Statement-II explains Statement-I.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 21:
1. In A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), the Supreme Court held that 'procedure established by law' means a procedure that must be just, fair and reasonable.
2. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Court held that the procedure under Article 21 must be just, fair and reasonable.
3. After Maneka Gandhi, a law depriving personal liberty must also satisfy the tests of Articles 14 and 19.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Gopalan took a narrow view: any procedure enacted by the legislature was enough. Maneka Gandhi treated Articles 14, 19 and 21 as interrelated, which brought in something close to due process.

questions.q:
Match the cases with the right they recognised under Article 21.
A. Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979)  B. Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985)  C. Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997)  D. K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
1. Speedy trial  2. Right to livelihood  3. Protection against sexual harassment at the workplace  4. Right to privacy
questions.e: Hussainara Khatoon, about undertrial prisoners, led to speedy trial. Olga Tellis (pavement dwellers) linked livelihood with life, Vishaka produced workplace guidelines, and Puttaswamy held privacy to be a fundamental right.

questions.q:
Statement-I: The right to die is not a part of the right to life under Article 21, as held in Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996).
Statement-II: In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court permitted passive euthanasia and recognised living wills.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Gian Kaur held that the right to life does not include the right to die and upheld the penal provision on abetment of suicide. Common Cause accepted the right to die with dignity only in the form of passive euthanasia, which is a different matter and does not explain the first.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017):
1. The case was decided by a bench of seven judges.
2. The Court held that the right to privacy is protected as part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and Part III generally.
3. The Court overruled the earlier holdings in M. P. Sharma and Kharak Singh, to the extent they denied a fundamental right to privacy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: A nine-judge bench, not seven, unanimously held privacy to be a fundamental right. It stemmed from the challenge to the Aadhaar scheme, and earlier decisions were overruled to the extent of the inconsistency.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 21A:
1. It was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.
2. It provides free and compulsory education to children aged six to fourteen years, in such manner as the State may by law determine.
3. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 came into force on 1 April 2010.
4. The 86th Amendment also amended Article 45 and added a fundamental duty on parents and guardians in Article 51A.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: All four statements are correct. Article 45 now directs the State to provide early childhood care and education to children below six years, and Article 51A(k) obliges parents to provide opportunities for education to children aged six to fourteen.

questions.q: Which one of the following judgments held that the right to education is a fundamental right under Article 21 but limited it to children up to the age of fourteen years?
o: Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992)
T. M. A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002)
Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984)
Unni Krishnan J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993)
questions.e: Mohini Jain (1992) treated education at all levels as part of Article 21. Unni Krishnan (1993) narrowed this to the age of fourteen and, after that, held it to be limited by the State's economic capacity. The 86th Amendment later gave statutory form to this through Article 21A.

questions.q: Which one of the following persons is NOT entitled to the protections of Article 22(1) and (2) against arrest and detention?
o: A citizen detained under a preventive detention law such as the National Security Act
A person arrested on a charge of theft
A foreign national, who is not an enemy alien, arrested for illegal stay
A woman arrested on a charge of cheating
questions.e: Article 22(3) denies the right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours and the right to a lawyer of choice to enemy aliens and to persons detained under preventive detention. Other persons arrested under ordinary law, including non-enemy foreigners, are covered.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding preventive detention under Article 22:
1. Detention beyond six months is permissible only on the report of an Advisory Board.
2. The Advisory Board consists of persons qualified to be judges of a High Court.
3. The proposal of the 44th Amendment to reduce the period of detention without an Advisory Board from three months to two months has not yet been brought into force.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The ordinary limit is three months, not six, beyond which the Advisory Board must give its report. The 44th Amendment's change to two months has not been notified, so the three-month period still applies.

questions.q:
Arrange the following preventive detention laws in the order in which they were enacted.
A. National Security Act  B. COFEPOSA  C. Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA)  D. Preventive Detention Act
questions.e: The Preventive Detention Act was enacted in 1950, MISA in 1971, COFEPOSA in 1974 and the National Security Act in 1980.

questions.q: Article 22(6) permits the authority making a preventive detention order to
o: detain a person without informing him of any grounds of detention
deny the detainee any opportunity to make a representation
extend the detention beyond three months in all cases without an Advisory Board
withhold facts which it considers to be against the public interest to disclose
questions.e: Under Article 22(5) the grounds must be communicated and the detainee must get the earliest opportunity to make a representation. Article 22(6) is the limited exception allowing the authority to withhold facts against the public interest.
